articles.title: [OPINION] From Super El Niño to the budget: What is the plan?
articles.summary: Why should citizens be forced to find the pieces of the puzzle instead of the government presenting the entire picture in the first place?

blocks.text: When mistakes have been made, we’re supposed to learn from them.
When it comes to transparency, however, many in the Bongbong Marcos administration seem to instead double down on avoiding transparency at a time when it is needed the most.
Case in point: the lack of a publicly accessible, updated Strategic El Niño Action Plan.

Hundreds of local government units have already declared a state of calamity. Agriculture and fisheries are already being affected. Our water security is at serious risk. Our health systems are already strained. And the peak of this Super El Niño has not even arrived yet.

Yes, it is understandable that this master plan needs to be flexible enough that some of its provisions could be reevaluated and even updated to improve responses to this pending crisis. Obviously, it also makes sense to have a division of labor across national agencies that would focus on responding to their covered sectors (i.e., agriculture, education, water, etc.).

Several agencies have already reported their strategies to deal with these impacts. For example, the Department of Agriculture proposed its P61.99-billion spending package for protecting food production and livelihoods. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources is monitoring the water situation across the country. Anticipatory action frameworks are being built to trigger responses before the peak.

But the lack of a publicly available and readily accessible overall Strategic El Niño Action Plan limits effective coordination among sectors and stakeholders in addressing these challenges. It prevents clear, efficient tracking of the quantity and effectiveness of expenditures, hindering the capacity to hold duty-bearers accountable.

Why should citizens be forced to find the pieces of the puzzle instead of the government presenting the entire picture in the first place? Why should we build our defenses against the Super El Niño without even knowing the overall blueprint?

Sadly, this is nowhere near the first time this administration has been shown lacking in its crisis communications. The same patterns emerge time and again: premature guarantees of readiness, inconsistent messaging, pronouncements of assistance without proper implementation, and centering much of its narrative on household-level responsibility.

This is not even the first time this year; remember how this government handled the energy crisis that is still ongoing these days? It is another reminder that our electricity bills could be increasing again soon because the peso is depreciating — that, and a bunch of factors, such as the government’s refusal to truly commit to transitioning away from fossil fuels.
It is more than fair to ask whose needs are really being addressed here. Speaking of needs…

No one should ever refuse to support bills that would mandate civil society and citizens’ participation in the national and local budgeting processes. After all, the budget that is intended for the Filipino people must be shaped by the Filipino people. It is a constitutional right of every citizen to be involved in decision-making processes, especially on an issue that involves their taxes, their well-being, and their future.

Yet there would not even be a need for this if there were a greener diet for public service instead of craving for pork — hard, soft, or however they like it figuratively cooked. There would be no need for this if there were no corruption in flood control projects or any other project.

No one in the government must ever be ignorant of the needs of the citizens they are sworn to serve. Yet the decisions made by the lower chamber of Congress in their version of the 2027 budget indicate they are not as aware of the needs of Filipinos as they should be.

Staying with the lens of the Super El Niño — projected to be the strongest in decades — reducing the budget for crop insurance, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund, or the entire health sector compared to their 2026 allotments just does not add up.

Aside from the procedural questions, there are other questions that must be asked: Do the allocations for constructing or rehabilitating water infrastructure projects go to communities that would be hit the earliest or the hardest by the pending droughts? Are these infrastructure projects designed to be truly resilient to current and future droughts, floods, and other hazards?

Public participation should never depend on who is in power. Transparency cannot depend on which lawmakers have thick enough skin for genuinely meaningful engagements. Accountability does not only apply after corruption has been exposed. Tears shed within air-conditioned hallways should not drown out the cries of the earth and the poor.

Whether it is the Super El Niño or any other issue, the public has the right and deserves to know not just how our money is being spent but also where, for what purpose, and for whom. We cannot expect citizens to trust duty-bearers who fail to answer these questions that are part of their mandate.
For anyone in public service, the best ability is accountability. For building a healthy democracy, the best currency is transparency. Never forget that. – Rappler.com
John Leo Algo is the national coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas.

articles.title: MIAA vows turnover of CCTV to NNIC in November after Dizon rebuke
articles.summary: The Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) on Friday promised to complete the turnover of the CCTV surveillance system to the Ninoy Aquino International Airport's (NAIA) private management by…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 5:32pm

The Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) on Friday promised to complete the turnover of the CCTV surveillance system to the Ninoy Aquino International Airport's (NAIA) private management by November 2026.

This comes hours after Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon lashed out at airport officials for failing to turn over the security camera system to the New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC). Dizon gave the officials until November to complete the turnover before people start getting fired.

"MIAA has already completed the final acceptance of the CCTV project and initiated the necessary arrangements for its formal turnover to NNIC in accordance with the NAIA Public-Private Partnership Concession Agreement," the agency said in a statement.
"MIAA is committed to working closely with NNIC to resolve the outstanding matters and complete the turnover within the period directed by the Secretary," it added.
The MIAA explained that it already initiated the turnover and acceptance agreement. It is also continuing CCTV repair and restoration efforts.

Earlier in the day, Dizon reprimanded the airport officials for failing to take responsibility over the CCTV matter after a theft was reported, especially since he already ordered the turnover a year ago during his initial stint as secretary of the Department of Transportation (DOTr).

Dizon was then appointed into the Department of Public Works and Highways, with Giovanni Lopez replacing him as Transport Secretary. Dizon and Lopez were switched Cabinet posts last Monday, with the former assuming his role as DOTr Secretary once more. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Is Vista Mall Santa Rosa next to go as the Villars’ debt deadlines loom?
articles.summary: The Villars aren’t saying much about the possible mall sale, but their long-delayed financials hint at billions in debt repayments that could be pushing them to part with some of their prized…

blocks.text: VILLAR PROPERTY. Vista Mall Santa Rosa in Laguna.
Rappler

The Villars aren’t saying much about the possible mall sale, but their long-delayed financials hint at billions in debt repayments that could be pushing them to part with some of their prized possessions

items: The Villar group is facing heavy debt repayments, leading to the potential sale of retail properties.
Vista Mall Santa Rosa, which opened in 2015, is reportedly being marketed with an asking price of P8 billion.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
First was AllDay in Libis. Now, possibly, Vista Mall Santa Rosa. As the Villar group faces heavy debt repayments, it seems their once-prized retail locations appear to be up for grabs.

The former AllDay supermarket site along C-5 in Libis, Quezon City, is now with Robinsons Retail Holdings Incorporated, a source with the Gokongwei group confirmed to Rappler. Shopwise is expected to open there by December, just a few steps away from RRHI’s office.

But that might just have been the start. An industry source familiar with the Villars hinted that more properties across the family’s businesses could change hands, with Vista Mall Santa Rosa possibly the latest to be shopped around.

Opened in April 2015 along the Santa Rosa-Tagaytay Road near Nuvali, Vista Mall Santa Rosa is a sprawling commercial complex housing an AllHome store, supermarket, cinemas, restaurants, and office spaces for BPO tenants. The property has reportedly been advertised online with an P8-billion asking price.
Senior officials at a prominent property brokerage told Rappler they were aware the mall was being marketed, although their firm had yet to approach the Villar group about a deal.

In a disclosure on Friday, October 30, Vista Malls said it had “not accepted any binding offer or entered into any definitive agreement” to sell Santa Rosa. It also said it does not comment on “preliminary, exploratory, or non-binding discussions.”

VistaREIT, another listed company in the group, offered its own narrow clarification, saying there was no definitive transaction involving a transfer of the assets into the real estate investment trust. Vista Land, meanwhile, said it was continually assessing property disposals and options to manage its liquidity.

In its 2025 audited financial statements, released only this October, Vista Land said it had already entered into agreements to dispose of unspecified investment properties after year-end and that the transactions were not recognized in the current set of financials. No properties were specifically identified. (READ: Villar’s Vista Land 2025 net income falls 59% as delayed figures surface)
Carefully chosen words, but none rule out talking to potential buyers.
Could these moves be coming as the Villars struggle to raise cash to meet billions in debt obligations due very soon?

blocks.caption: DEBT. Tables showing the sizable loans that Vista Land must repay in the coming years. Tables from Vista Land’s 2025 audited financial statements

blocks.text: The Villars’ debt pressure is well documented. Vista Land’s 2025 audited report alone identified:

items: Around P21.33 billion in notes and bonds scheduled to mature in 2026, based on balances at the end of 2025
$420 million* (P26.8 billion) in overseas notes maturing in July 2027
P2 billion in corporate notes being repaid in installments through March 2027
P2 billion in retail bonds due August 2027

blocks.text: Vista Land’s major shareholders themselves stepped in to finance the company, extending P22.49 billion in interest-bearing loans in 2025 that were used to repay maturing debt.
And that’s just what Vista Land’s (long-delayed) books tell us. Several other listed Villar companies have yet to release their overdue financial statements.
Who knows what other surprises could be hiding in there? – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Undas is the Filipino term for the observance of All Saints’ Day on November 1 and All Souls’ Day on November 2, when families remember and honor deceased loved ones.

It is a time for Filipinos to remember and honor loved ones who have passed away, as families gather in cemeteries, travel to their home provinces, and observe traditions that celebrate the lives of the departed.

As technology becomes part of everyday life, some Filipinos also observe Undas online by sharing tributes, photos and memories of their departed loved ones on social media, while others join virtual masses and online prayer services.

blocks.text: EXPLAINER: What is the Free Funeral Services Act?
Did you know that the government is mandated by law to provide free funeral services to poor Filipinos who cannot afford a decent burial for their loved ones?
On September 28, 2025, Republic Act No. 12309, or the “Free Funeral Services Act,” lapsed into law after remaining unacted upon for 30 days without the signature of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
This law institutionalized the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s (DSWD) funeral assistance initiative through its Aid to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program.

Under RA 12309, free funeral services must be extended to families in crisis situations, as determined by the DSWD, including indigent families, those affected by calamities or disasters, and individuals facing emergency circumstances that prevent them from affording dignified burial services.
How does the law grant its beneficiaries a decent funeral?
Beneficiary
According to the Free Funeral Services Act, the service is provided to “poor families per death of a family member.”
The law defines “poor families” as those whose income falls below the poverty threshold as defined by the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development.
This classification also includes those unable to meet basic needs, such as food, health, education, and housing, as defined under the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act.

For 2025, the poverty threshold was set at a national average of P14,634 per month, up from P13,873 in 2023. Meaning, this figure represents the minimum income required for a family to meet its basic food and non-food needs.
Under this 2025 threshold, a family whose monthly income falls below the threshold is considered poor.
How to avail the assistance?
Free funeral services may be obtained from accredited funeral establishments nationwide that offer a standardized indigent funeral package.
“Free funeral services shall be provided to poor families per death of a family member by accredited funeral establishment anywhere in the country,” the law said.

Funeral establishments refer to licensed businesses that provide services such as funeral parlors, chapels, and similar facilities used for preparing, transporting, storing, and caring for the deceased prior to burial or cremation.
The free funeral package covers the preparation of funeral documents, embalming, burial, cremation, inurnment, transportation, and the provision of a casket or urn.
To avail of the indigent funeral package, under the law, the bereaved family or an authorized representative must present the following requirements:

items: Valid identification card of the claimant or beneficiary;
Death certificate issued by the hospital or city/municipal health office, or certification from the tribal chieftain;
Funeral contract signed by the representative of the deceased's family, the funeral establishment, and an authorized DSWD personnel; and
Social care study prepared by any registered social worker

blocks.text: At present, the DSWD also requires additional documents depending on the specific services requested. Further details are available through the DSWD AICS Funeral Assistance Portal.
Upon the approval of the DSWD Regional Director, the agency pays the funeral establishment for the indigent package rendered to the beneficiary.

“The payment will be based on the stipulations of the signed contract between the representative of the deceased's family, the funeral establishment, and the authorized DSWD personnel,” the law notes.
Penalties for violations
Funeral establishments that refuse to provide free funeral services face a maximum fine of P400,000, alongside the revocation of their operating license.
Meanwhile, individuals who fraudulently avail of the free funeral service face up to six months of imprisonment and a maximum fine of P500,000.

Data from the DSWD show that from 2014 to September 2025, the agency extended burial assistance to families of 1,439,160 individuals, releasing a total of P10.9 million through the AICS program. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News
Cebu Archbishop: Honor departed loved ones through peaceful, prayerful visit to cemeteries
Cebu Archbishop Alberto "Abet" Uy has issued a "gentle reminder" asking the faithful to ensure a "peaceful and prayerful" observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day or Undas this weekend.

"As we bring flowers, light candles, and offer prayers, let us remember one important thing: the cemetery is sacred ground. It is not simply a place we visit once a year. It is a place of prayer and remembrance, where our loved ones rest as we await the resurrection," he said.

"For this reason, I appeal to everyone: Let us keep our cemeteries peaceful and prayerful. Let us avoid unnecessary noise, loud music, shouting, and boisterous laughter. Families will naturally gather and share stories, but let us always be mindful that beside us may be someone quietly praying, grieving, or simply spending a few precious moments with a loved one who has gone before them. Our joy should never disturb another person’s prayer," he added.
Archbishop Uy also called on the people to "keep our cemeteries clean and care for our common home."
An advocate of environmental protection, he encouraged cemetery visitors to bring their own tumbler or water container, use reusable bags, and avoid single-use plastics.
Do not leave trash at the site, use designated garbage bins, and do not burn waste.

"As Christians, caring for creation is also part of our faith. And perhaps one beautiful way of honoring those who have gone before us is to care for the place where they rest. So when we leave the cemetery, may we leave nothing behind except our prayers, gratitude, and love," said Uy.

"Let us honor our departed loved ones. Let us respect sacred ground. Let us respect those who come to pray. And together, let us care for our common home. May God bless you and your families." — BAP, GMA News
When no one bids the dead goodbye
The smell hit Rhiannah Sta. Ana before she ever laid eyes on the cadavers.
A first year physical therapy student at a Metro Manila university, Sta. Ana likened the pungent odor to the strong smell of hair dye at a salon.

These bodies have been preserved with a chemical called formalin, Sta. Ana explained. While their facilitators told them what to expect, nothing could quite prepare the students once the covers were removed and the cadavers were revealed for the first time.

Many were taken aback. After all, the bodies before them used to be living people, Sta. Ana said. Yet to the students, they were strangers, their identities lost to time. She found herself wondering: Who were they when they were alive? Where did they live? What were their names?
Historically, cultures all around the world have different ceremonies to commemorate their dead. These days, people typically bury their loved ones or cremate them, giving them the final respects.
But what happens when someone dies, and there is no one left to claim their body, let alone bid them goodbye?
Responsibility over the dead

Presidential Decree No. 856, or the Code of Sanitation of the Philippines, outlines several rules on the proper handling of human remains, including the provision allowing the use of unclaimed bodies for research.
“Unclaimed remains may be used by medical schools and scientific institutions for studies and research subject to the rules and regulations prescribed by the Department,” the decree read.

The Department of Health would later update and elaborate the presidential decree through Administrative Order 2010 - 0033, or the “Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations of the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines Chapter XXI Disposal of Dead Persons."
Under the rules, funeral parlors or embalming establishments are not allowed to hold unclaimed bodies for more than 60 days.

While some might find the thought unpleasant, there have been many instances of bodies seemingly being abandoned by their relatives and friends. In 2022, the bodies of 176 of Bilibid inmates were unclaimed at the Eastern Funeral Homes — many of them had to be buried because they were already rotting.
Based on the data provided by the Bureau of Corrections (BuCor), there are 1,144 unclaimed bodies from 2020-2025 in the New Bilibid Prison.
The recorded unclaimed bodies are as follows:

items: 2020: 258 cadavers
2021: 285 cadavers
2022: 187 cadavers
2023: 128 cadavers
2024: 135 cadavers
2025: 151 cadavers

blocks.text: Correctional Technical / Corrections Chief Superintendent (CT/CSUPT) Ma. Cecilia Villanueva, BuCor Deputy Director General for Reformation, explained that families are unable to claim the deceased persons deprived of liberty (PDL) because their homes are far.
"Usually yung mga tawid-dagat, yung malalayo, Visayas, Mindanao, but we send letters," Villanueva told GMA News Online.
(Those people cross the seas; they are from Visayas and Mindanao, but we send letters.)
Once a PDL is declared dead, the body is brought to Eastern Funeral Home in Muntinlupa City for documentation, while the Bureau of Corrections contacts the deceased’s family.
However, in some cases, family members cannot be contacted, or no one claims the bodies due to financial constraints, while others just retrieve the death certificates.
Unclaimed bodies are then buried in the New Bilibid Prison Cemetery, also in Muntinlupa City.
“Kasi kahit sabihin naman natin na mga PDL, they have the same rights as any public person,” Villanueva said.
“Meron din silang dignidad kahit pa naman sabihin natin na mga PDL ’yan. May dignity pa rin in their death," she added.
(Even though they are PDLs, they have the same rights as any public person. They still have dignity, even in death.)
BuCor data showed the highest number of unclaimed bodies in 2021 (285 cadavers) and 2020 (258 cadavers), the years when the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted operations worldwide.
“Yung period namin for [claiming the deceased persons] lumampas nga sa 60 days. Kasi nga, may mga limitations sa movement,” Villanueva said.
(Our period for claiming the deceased exceeded 60 days due to restrictions on movement.)
“Kahit nga yung cremated, yung iba hindi na nila claim yung remains ng relatives nila,” Villanueva said, adding that PDLs who died from the coronavirus were immediately cremated.
(Even those that were cremated, some relatives were unable to claim them.)
According to the BuCor data, 89 cremated bodies were claimed while 23 were unclaimed.
Left behind

Quezon City’s Burial Assistance Program serves indigent residents by providing free burial services. Vivs Funeral Homes is one of the funeral parlors accredited by the local government in the project.
Vivs Funeral Homes Operations Manager Larry Leccio said that although rare, there have been instances when they had to bury an unclaimed body.
There are various reasons why bodies go unclaimed, Leccio explained. In some cases, they belong to impoverished people who die on the streets and are brought to hospitals.
“Itong isang patay ay dinala ng pamilya niya sa ospital doon sa East Avenue. Tapos, hindi na binalikan. Tapos hindi na mahanap yung pamilya,” Leccio said.
(One of the dead was brought by the family to the hospital there in East Avenue. After that, they did not come back. And the family could no longer be found.)

The process typically began at the hospital, according to Leccio. The hospital then alerts the barangay, which makes a report. Details about the found body are then circulated in newspapers for 30 days in hopes of finding a claimant. During those 30 days, the body remains at the morgue of the funeral home.
However, once the body hits the 60-day mark, the local government needs to act on the matter.

Since the Quezon City local government has a free funeral service program, a barangay representative will be interviewed by the city’s Social Services Development Department on behalf of the unclaimed body.
Once local government officials handle all the necessary documentation, the funeral parlor can process the death certificate.

In case that no one knows the body’s name, the cadavers are simply issued a case number and labeled as “unknown” before being buried in a public cemetery. Their tombstones would also be labeled as such, Leccio said.
There would be no ceremonies for the body.
“Direct na libing na po siya. Wala na po siyang pamisa,” Leccio said. (It is a direct burial. There will be no masses.)
The dead as a teacher

Despite the initial shock of seeing the cadavers before them, Sta. Ana said that the students would eventually get used to them because of how invaluable they were as learning instruments — they could even freely go in and out of the laboratory where the cadavers were just to study them.
As the semester went on, the students got used to dealing with the cadavers. So much so that they almost forget that bodies used to be people.

“We still have to remember to be respectful to it, kasi nga, habang na nasasanay ka sa nakikita mo sa harapan mo, nakakalimutan mo na this was a person, this is a person we're dealing with, kahit hindi na siya nagsasalita,” Sta. Ana said.

(We still have to remember to be respectful to it, because while you get used to seeing it in front of you, you forget that this was a person, this is a person we’re dealing with, even if they no longer speak.)
As a result, the students would always begin their sessions with the bodies with a prayer, offering them gratitude.
They had also given the anonymous bodies names, and spoke to them as if they were still alive.
“Mami” was the name of the cadaver assigned to Sta. Ana and her group. She still has a personal bracelet on her wrist, which the students kept on.
Whenever an incision needed to be made, or if skin needed to be pulled back, the students would inform the cadaver that it could hurt and apologize to them.

“We talk to them as if they are still alive, so even if we know that they are physically not with us, we still find a way to talk to them and say ‘thank you’, and say ‘sorry’... it helps us humanize the experience,” Sta. Ana said.

While they knew nothing of the stories of the bodies before them, sometimes, the bodies themselves offered signs of how they died. Both the teachers and students could make their own inferences on how the cadavers wound up dead. Sta. Anna recounted that one of the first bodies she saw had red marks around the neck.

Regardless of how the bodies ended up before the students, one thing was certain: they were invaluable teachers. As physical therapy students, they had to become familiar with human anatomy. And these bodies could teach them things that no book ever could, Sta. Ana said.
They would often go around looking at different types of bodies just to learn more, she added.
Sta. Ana hopes of becoming a doctor one day, a path that would likely introduce her to even more cadavers.
“We recognize that we’re learning so much through their bodies and we understand that they make significant contributions to our education as physical therapists,” Sta. Ana said.
While the bodies that reached Sta. Ana and her classmates were anonymous, it was unlikely that they were prisoners.
Villanueva said the agency has not been providing cadavers to be dissected in medical schools after they were flagged by human rights groups.
“I started in 1998. Parang around that time na pinagbawal ng human rights yung paggamit ng body para sa mga medical schools,” Villanueva shared.
(I started in 1998. Around that time, it was around that time, I think, that the use of bodies for medical school purposes was prohibited after being flagged by human rights groups.)
“Marami naman kaming letter requests from medical schools na hindi namin na-approve,” she added.
Currently, BuCor is looking into building more buildings across the country to decongest existing detention facilities and bring PDLs closer to their families.
“More regional prison facilities [kasi] dapat yung nandito, yung taga-NCR, yung malapit. Eh hindi eh. Marami dito na taga-tawid-dagat pa rin,” Villanueva said.
(BuCor is working on regional prison facilities because PDLs from NCR should be detained here, but that’s not the case. Many PDLs here are from far away areas.)
The Holy Body
We are all made according to God’s likeness, according to Father John Paulo Bautista of the Mary Immaculate Parish in Dasmariñas City.

“The Church teaches very clearly that everybody, every Christian, Catholics or not, every human person, whether it is unclaimed or claimed bodies, we bear the image of God,” Bautista said in an interview.

However, this does not mean that priests could simply bless abandoned bodies, as they may not be certain if the corpses were Catholic when they were still alive, Bautista explained. Priests would need the permission of the deceased’s kin to bless the body.

Bautista recounted a time when he saw a motorcycle rider who died in a road crash incident. While he was initially inclined to give the body blessing, he had to stop and think. Would it have been an act of charity? Would he have to wait for the family?
Priests were not strictly prohibited from blessing a body that they were unsure of being Catholic however, Bautista explained. But it was still discouraged.
In cases where the body is used as a learning instrument — as was the case with the physical therapy students — Bautista maintained that it should be done morally.
“It should be done in a right way, legal way, in a moral way, at the same time, with a reverence to the body,” Bautista said.
“The human body is sacred,” he added.
There are a few ways to honor the unclaimed dead, according to Bautista. For Catholics, they could offer a Mass, prayer, or even the act of remembrance.
But what if there was no one left to remember the dead? Bautista said that Catholics could offer a prayer for a soul in purgatory.

“The Church is praying for them, in Masses, they are remembered… If you will pray for them, generally, we could say prayers for the souls in purgatory, and for those who have not attained a peaceful, holy, or blessed death,” Bautista said. —Jean Mangaluz and Mariel Celine Serquiña with GMA News Research/Joviland Rita/ LDF, GMA News

Prime minister in Glasgow to meet with Scottish and Welsh leaders to talk about ‘next stage of devolution’

Andy Burnham has admitted

blocks.text: Key events

items: 12m agoBurnham admits he would have liked more radical first budget
18m agoBurnham says he wants to offer more ‘regional empowerment’ ahead of devolution summit with Scottish and Welsh leaders

blocks.text: Burnham admits he would have liked more radical first budget
Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country, Kiran Stacey reports.
Burnham says he wants to offer more ‘regional empowerment’ ahead of devolution summit with Scottish and Welsh leaders

Good morning. Andy Burnham is in Glasgow today for a meeting with the leaders from Scotland and Wales and he says he wants to use it to talk about “the next stage of devolution”. According to the overnight briefing from No 10, he is less interested in giving more powers to the devolved parliaments and more interested in promoting “regional empowerment” in their countries.
In his pre-summit statement, Burnham says:

double quotation markThrough No 10 North, we are rewiring the state. I want to make sure every city and region in the United Kingdom is part of that. Today I’ll be making an offer to the governments of each nation. Put politics aside and work in partnership with the UK government to develop models of regional empowerment that ensure communities can use their own strengths to unlock their potential. This is the next stage of devolution. Together, there is no limit to what we can achieve.

Burnham is speaking at a time when Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have since the May elections (when Plaid Cymru won in Wales) for the first time had first ministers from nationalist parties that want to break away from the UK. John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, will be at the meeting today. But Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister from Northern Ireland won’t be there. She holds power jointly with a DUP deputy, and both of them have to stay away because the DUP has vetoed their attendance due to an ongoing row about Drumcree. Some officials will attend instead.

Downing Street says at today’s meeting Burnham “will say that devolution by default shouldn’t be about the transfer of powers from one parliament to another but should go deeper within nations to empower all places and communities who know best what they need to grow and access opportunities.”
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Andy Burnham chairs a meeting of the national economic council in Glasgow.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
Afternoon (UK time): Ed Miliband is attending a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta in the US.

“We talk to them as if they are still alive, so even if we know that they are physically not with us, we still find a way to talk to them and say ‘thank you’, and say ‘sorry’... it helps us humanize the experience,” Sta. Ana said.

While they knew nothing of the stories of the bodies before them, sometimes, the bodies themselves offered signs of how they died. Both the teachers and students could make their own inferences on how the cadavers wound up dead. Sta. Anna recounted that one of the first bodies she saw had red marks around the neck.

Regardless of how the bodies ended up before the students, one thing was certain: they were invaluable teachers. As physical therapy students, they had to become familiar with human anatomy. And these bodies could teach them things that no book ever could, Sta. Ana said.
They would often go around looking at different types of bodies just to learn more, she added.
Sta. Ana hopes of becoming a doctor one day, a path that would likely introduce her to even more cadavers.
“We recognize that we’re learning so much through their bodies and we understand that they make significant contributions to our education as physical therapists,” Sta. Ana said.
While the bodies that reached Sta. Ana and her classmates were anonymous, it was unlikely that they were prisoners.
Villanueva said the agency has not been providing cadavers to be dissected in medical schools after they were flagged by human rights groups.
“I started in 1998. Parang around that time na pinagbawal ng human rights yung paggamit ng body para sa mga medical schools,” Villanueva shared.
(I started in 1998. Around that time, it was around that time, I think, that the use of bodies for medical school purposes was prohibited after being flagged by human rights groups.)
“Marami naman kaming letter requests from medical schools na hindi namin na-approve,” she added.
Currently, BuCor is looking into building more buildings across the country to decongest existing detention facilities and bring PDLs closer to their families.
“More regional prison facilities [kasi] dapat yung nandito, yung taga-NCR, yung malapit. Eh hindi eh. Marami dito na taga-tawid-dagat pa rin,” Villanueva said.
(BuCor is working on regional prison facilities because PDLs from NCR should be detained here, but that’s not the case. Many PDLs here are from far away areas.)
The Holy Body
We are all made according to God’s likeness, according to Father John Paulo Bautista of the Mary Immaculate Parish in Dasmariñas City.

“The Church teaches very clearly that everybody, every Christian, Catholics or not, every human person, whether it is unclaimed or claimed bodies, we bear the image of God,” Bautista said in an interview.

However, this does not mean that priests could simply bless abandoned bodies, as they may not be certain if the corpses were Catholic when they were still alive, Bautista explained. Priests would need the permission of the deceased’s kin to bless the body.

Bautista recounted a time when he saw a motorcycle rider who died in a road crash incident. While he was initially inclined to give the body blessing, he had to stop and think. Would it have been an act of charity? Would he have to wait for the family?
Priests were not strictly prohibited from blessing a body that they were unsure of being Catholic however, Bautista explained. But it was still discouraged.
In cases where the body is used as a learning instrument — as was the case with the physical therapy students — Bautista maintained that it should be done morally.
“It should be done in a right way, legal way, in a moral way, at the same time, with a reverence to the body,” Bautista said.
“The human body is sacred,” he added.
There are a few ways to honor the unclaimed dead, according to Bautista. For Catholics, they could offer a Mass, prayer, or even the act of remembrance.
But what if there was no one left to remember the dead? Bautista said that Catholics could offer a prayer for a soul in purgatory.

“The Church is praying for them, in Masses, they are remembered… If you will pray for them, generally, we could say prayers for the souls in purgatory, and for those who have not attained a peaceful, holy, or blessed death,” Bautista said. —With GMA News Research/Joviland Rita/ LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos to new Bangsamoro MPs: Serve with humility, good governance
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday called on the newly elected members of the Bangsamoro parliament to serve the people with humility and honor those who fought for peace through…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 5:06pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday called on the newly elected members of the Bangsamoro parliament to serve the people with humility and honor those who fought for peace through good governance.
This, as the President attended the inaugural session of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliament at the Bangsamoro Government Center in Cotabato City.
Marcos said that the first session of the BARMM parliament is not just a victory for Mindanao, but the entire country.

“For decades, generations wondered if this day would ever come. Today, we welcome the inaugural session of the first elected Bangsamoro Parliament. This formally ends the seven-year transition under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority and marks the beginning of the region’s first regular parliamentary government,” he said.
“Truly, this is a victory for our Bangsamoro brethren. It is a victory for Mindanao. It is a victory for the entire Filipino nation,” he added.

The President also noted that the event serves as a milestone in the peace process between the national government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), “marking the transition from armed struggle to peaceful democratic governance.”
He however, acknowledged that the path leading up to the conduct of the inaugural session was “long and painful,” with families suffering and losing loved ones during years of conflict.
Under the new phase of parliamentary governance, Marcos said leaders must uphold unity, statesmanship, and cooperation to build a more peaceful and progressive BARMM.

“A stable government means enacting laws and delivering programs and services responsive to the needs of the Bangsamoro people. It also means using public resources efficiently and transparently to create economic opportunities and strengthen regional development,” he explained.
“Above all, it means ensuring that the dividends of peace are felt in the daily lives of every Bangsamoro family,” he continued.
Marcos also committed that the national government will continue to expand economic opportunities for Mindanao, and will continue to support the Bangsamoro autonomy and democratic institutions.

“To the people of the Bangsamoro, the national government stands with you. Your success is the success of the country. Hinding-hindi namin kayo pababayaan (we will never abandon you),” the President said.
The BARMM held its first parliamentary elections on September 14, with a final voter turnout of 84.34%, representing 2,018,478 voters out of the region’s 2.393 million registered voters.

The 80 newly elected Parliament members assumed office today, October 30, and are set to elect the region’s chief minister. The first elected officials will serve a five-year term until June 30, 2031.

Under Republic Act No. 11054 or the Bangsamoro Organic Law, the Parliament will elect the Chief Minister by a majority vote of at least 41 of its 80 members. The Chief Minister will lead the regional government and advance its development priorities, subject to parliamentary oversight. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: UK house prices grow at slowest pace in two years as mortgage rates rise
articles.summary:
Sluggish growth of 0.5% in October comes as higher borrowing costs put break on market

UK house prices grew by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two…

blocks.text: UK house prices grew by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years, as higher mortgage rates put off potential buyers.
The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566 in October, flat on the previous month and down from 0.8% in the year to September, according to the lender Nationwide.
The slowdown in the market comes as buyers face higher borrowing costs. This month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years.
The average stood at 5.99% on Thursday, according to the financial information provider Moneyfacts, while the average two-year rate was not far behind at 5.97%.
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.

While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week the monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.
Robert Gardner, the chief economist at Nationwide, said the Middle East conflict had fed concerns around inflation, driving up expectations of higher interest rates.
Property prices are likely to fall further, he said. “Surveyors report that new buyer inquiries remain weak.
“Consumer sentiment dipped noticeably in October, with households becoming less confident about the outlook for the general economy as well as their own financial situation in the year ahead.”
Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, added that the impact of rising mortgage costs “eclipses any support measure announced in this week’s budget”.
after newsletter promotion

This week the chancellor, John Healey, confirmed the government’s new £4.7bn Your First Home scheme, which is designed to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”.

Bill added: “The absence of major shocks from the chancellor may produce a modest relief bounce in coming months. However, asking prices will need to reflect the much tougher financial landscape that buyers face.”

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said the government’s new scheme could provide a “modest boost” to the market but that prices were likely to remain subdued next year.

articles.title: Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta to close
articles.summary:
Newspaper whose former editor won Nobel peace prize says pressure from Russian authorities has forced it to shut

The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announced on Friday that it…

blocks.text: The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it is closing, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.

“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” the editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said in a video statement published on YouTube on Friday. “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”

Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile. Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed by Moscow as a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Sokolov said: “Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”

blocks.caption: Sergei Sokolov, the Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief.  Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: This month Sokolov was taken in for questioning and Russian authorities searched his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Roldugin was detained and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”, without any details being given. He pleaded not guilty, according to the state RIA news agency.
Roldugin is awaiting trial while under house arrest that has been extended until 10 November, according to Novaya Gazeta.

Russia has intensified its crackdown on independent news outlets since its offensive on Ukraine in February 2022. Novaya Gazeta cut down production inside Russia after the offensive began. Authorities revoked its media licence the same year.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

articles.title: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says
articles.summary:
Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan

The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in…

blocks.text: The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.

Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.

The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.
With food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.

Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.

He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.
“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.

His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”

blocks.caption: Fuel shortages are threatening neonatal intensive care units in Taiz, where 120 health centres have been suspended.  Photograph: Hamza Mustafa/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.

He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.

People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.

Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.

blocks.caption: Rubbish is piling up in the city’s streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible. Photograph: Hamza Mustafa/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.

Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.
“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos didn’t vow to stay in Palace till flood mess ends
articles.summary: Article 7 of the 1987 Constitution limits an elected president to a single six-year term with no eligibility for re-election

blocks.text: Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will not leave the Palace until the flood control scandal is resolved.
Why we fact-checked this: Viral Philippines, a Facebook page with 321,000 followers, posted a supposed quote card of Marcos dated October 24.
The quote read, “Hindi ako aalis sa Malacañang hangga’t hindi naaayos ang problema sa flood control.” (I will not leave Malacañang until the flood control problem is resolved.)
The page captioned it, “Forever na ito sa Malacañang.” (He’s here to stay in Malacañang forever)
The post garnered 23,700 reactions, 4,800 comments, and 522 shares as of writing. Commenters also believed the quote and questioned Marcos’ capability to address the flood control scandal.
The facts: No official records or statements confirm that Marcos made this remark. Nor is there any indication that he intends to remain in office beyond his term to resolve the flood control issue.
In addition, Article 7 of the 1987 Constitution limits an elected president to a single six-year term with no eligibility for reelection.

The President has faced scrutiny over the administration’s handling of the issue. In July, he dismissed calls for his resignation over allegations that the government’s response to flood control problems has been too slow.

He did not voice plans to extend his term; he instead said, “I cannot say that we have done enough because we are not done yet. Unfortunately, the more we look, the more we find. And it is already going back beyond my administration, beyond my term.”

In his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA), Marcos announced that P800 million worth of assets out of P20 billion for flood control funds have been recovered since flagging them in his previous SONA.
In September, Marcos said that a decades-old flood control master plan for Luzon is finally being implemented.
Flood control arrests: After the 2025 SONA, multiple investigations have resulted in the arrests of high-profile individuals linked to flood control corruption.

These include contractor Sarah Discaya, Senator Jinggoy Estrada, former Department of Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan (released after being announced as turning into a state witness), and Congressman and Marcos’ cousin Martin Romualdez.

Meanwhile, former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co has been on the run and out of the country since 2025. He’s facing another graft and malversation case filed by the Office of the Ombudsman in August, besides a similar case filed before the Sandiganbayan in November 2025.

Extending or stepping down: Rappler has debunked numerous false claims surrounding Marcos’ presidential term — either having to do with not stepping down or changing the Constitution to stay in office:

items: FACT CHECK: Contrary to claim, Marcos has no plans to resign
FACT CHECK: Marcos did not say he wants another 6-year presidential term
FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim is ‘fake news,’ Malacañang says
FACT CHECK: Marcos statement claiming to cancel 2028 election is taken out of context

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: North Korean hackers behind $6.3-B Binance crypto theft – report
articles.summary: North Korean hacking unit TraderTraitor targets Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, moving the funds out in about 20 minutes

blocks.text: CRYPTO. Bitcoin cryptocurrency representation is pictured on a keyboard in front of binary code in this illustration taken September 24, 2021.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
North Korean hacking unit TraderTraitor targets Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, moving the funds out in about 20 minutes

MANILA, Philippines – TRM Labs, an AI investigations company and blockchain analyst group, said in a report on Thursday, October 29 (October 30, Philippine time), that the theft of $6.3 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Binance could be attributed to a hacking unit from North Korea.
In a blogpost explaining its findings, TRM said the premier North Korean hacking unit TraderTraitor was behind the attack on Binance, basing the assessment on intelligence sources it has.
TraderTraitor apparently targeted Binance wallets on 10 blockchains, moving the funds out in about 20 minutes.
While Binance has been able to freeze affected assets of about $3 billion with the help of its partners, there’s no word yet on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion

blocks.caption: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3-billion security breach

blocks.text: TraderTraitor was also behind the $1.5-billion heist of ByBit, another cryptocurrency exchange, in 2025.
TRM added that several features of the Binance attack “match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack” and an attack on the KelpDAO exchange in 2026.
TRM said the theft of Binance “is the largest crypto theft on record.”
“Even after the stablecoin freezes, the amount the attacker still holds exceeds any previous theft,” the firm added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 5 DPWH Bulacan engineers suspended over P118-M anomalous flood control projects
articles.summary: The DPWH engineers face charges of grave misconduct, serious dishonesty, and gross neglect of duty in connection with alleged irregularities in three flood control projects worth P188.9 million in…

blocks.text: The DPWH engineers face charges of grave misconduct, serious dishonesty, and gross neglect of duty in connection with alleged irregularities in three flood control projects worth P188.9 million in Baliuag, Bulacan

items: The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the preventive suspension of five public works engineers from Bulacan's first district engineering office due to their alleged involvement in corrupt flood control projects.
The suspended engineers face serious charges including grave misconduct and gross neglect of duty related to irregularities in three flood control projects worth P188.9 million.
The investigation is part of a larger corruption scandal involving multiple officials from the Department of Public Works and Highways, with some already dismissed and others detained.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman ordered the preventive suspension of five public works engineers from Bulacan’s first district engineering office (DEO) over their alleged involvement in anomalous flood control projects.
Those subjected to preventive suspension are the following project engineers:

items: Irene D. Ontingco
Kevin A. Geronimo
John Michael E. Ramos
Bernardo P. Villafuerte
Michelle C. Cruz

blocks.text: In a statement released on Friday, October 30, the Ombudsman said the government engineers were suspended without pay for a period not exceeding six months, pending the resolution of administrative cases against them.

They face charges of grave misconduct, serious dishonesty, and gross neglect of duty in connection with alleged irregularities in three flood control projects worth P188.9 million in Baliuag, Bulacan.

“To facilitate the implementation of the contracts and the disbursement of public funds, complainant maintains that respondents falsified documents relating to contract implementation, inspection, acceptance, billing and payment to create the false impression that the contractual and legal prerequisites had been satisfied,” the order from Ombudsman reads.

The Bulacan 1st DEO has figured prominently in the flood control corruption scandal. It was the former workplace of dismissed Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials Brice Hernandez and Henry Alcantara.

In his testimony before a Senate panel investigating flood control corruption in September 2025, Hernandez claimed that all projects implemented by the Bulacan 1st DEO from 2019 to 2025 were substandard.

Hernandez and Alcantara, along with other DPWH officials Jaypee Mendoza, Arjay Domasig, and Juanito C. Mendoza, were also named in the administrative complaint. However, they were not covered by the preventive suspension order – they have already been dismissed from the DPWH.

The Ombudsman also ordered the preventive suspension of DPWH engineer Norberto L. Santos and administrative officer Floralyn Y. Simbulan. However, the implementation of the order against them was rendered moot because Santos and Simbulan have already been detained in Quezon City and Bulacan, respectively.
Meanwhile, state auditors Cinderella Esperanza A. Santos and Madonna S. Atencion, who were also named as respondents in the case, were not preventively suspended.
According to the Ombudsman, there was no showing that their continued presence in office would pose a risk of evidence tampering or hamper the ongoing investigation.

Others who also figured in the case are former DPWH administrative officer Evelyn T. De Jesus, former engineer Ernesto C. Galang, former materials engineer Vicente G. Calderon, and former project engineer Merg Jaron C. Laus. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age
articles.summary: On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' cannot live from their pensions.

image.caption: Many of the 'guest workers' worked underground in coal minesImage: Guenay Ulutuncok/akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.
At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.

By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned the factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."

blocks.caption: Baden-Württemberg State Premier Cem Özdemir is the most prominent German politician of Turkish descentImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Some upward mobility among migrants, but discrimination a big problem

According to Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that. Even 65 years later, he told DW, there is still a great deal of discrimination in Germany against people of Turkish descent. However, he points out that the recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story: "We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.

Uslucan is a perfect example: His father came to Berlin after 1971 and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, he brought his wife and two sons to join him. Haci-Halil Uslucan earned his Ph.D. in psychology and is now a professor of Modern Turkish Studies at the University of Duisburg-Essen. One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement — an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called 'guest workers': loneliness. But it is not just loneliness that is increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.

"Studies show that poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants — between 25% and 30% compared to 12% to 14% among Germans. The disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor." They are also twice as likely to become unemployed ten years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan. "In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."
Three perspectives: What does German citizenship mean?
Pensions €360 lower among Turkish citizens in Germany

A special analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, has come up with some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €360 ($403) less in pension benefits than German pensioners. At the end of 2025, the figure was €890 compared to €1,250 per month. Even more troubling is that in June 2026 more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).

Social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW that many of the 'guest workers' came to Germany were not at the start of their working lives and were therefore able to contribute less to their pension fund. "But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.

With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many also lost their jobs. "There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."

blocks.caption: Coal mines in the Ruhr Valley closed during deindustrialization throwing many out of work. Some are now museumsImage: Stefan Ziese/picture alliance/Zoonar

blocks.text: Few chances for migrant workers to train

Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants. In her view, the fact that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty is a major problem in Germany. "This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, the situation would be even sorrier."

Even the opportunity to earn a few extra euros during retirement is often unavailable to many older people of Turkish origin. Either because their qualifications — which are often limited — are insufficient, or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit. According to figures from the German Federal Employment Agency, their employment rate is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%). Söhn says: "Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training." For the guest workers, on the other hand, there were no continuing education initiatives. "The people who did these tough jobs — which are always necessary for any economy — paid for it with their health."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Maharlika Fund’s NGCP deal collapses nearly 2 years after Marcos’ blessing
articles.summary: Once touted as Maharlika's maiden investment, the deal was supposed to give the government board seats at the country’s power grid operator. Instead, it marks another setback in MIC's sluggish…

blocks.text: Once touted as Maharlika's maiden investment, the deal was supposed to give the government board seats at the country’s power grid operator. Instead, it marks another setback in MIC's sluggish investment rollout.

items: The Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC) has withdrawn from a planned P19.7-billion investment in Synergy Grid and Development Philippines (SGP), which would have increased government influence over the power grid.
SGP confirmed that MIC's decision was due to a change in their strategic direction and will not affect SGP's finances or the operations of the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP).

The canceled deal was intended to give MIC a 20% stake in SGP, allowing for greater government oversight, but comes as MIC's CEO approaches the end of his term and amid ongoing challenges for the sovereign wealth fund.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC) has backed out of its planned P19.7-billion investment in Synergy Grid and Development Philippines (SGP), abandoning for now a deal that would have given the government a bigger say in the operations of the country’s power grid.
In a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange on Friday, October 30, SGP said MIC had informed them that it would no longer pursue the transaction for now.

“MIC has decided not to proceed with the transaction for the time being due to their current strategic direction,” SGP said, adding that the decision would have no impact on its finances or the operations of the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP).

SGP is a listed holding company that indirectly controls 60% of NGCP’s voting shares, with an effective equity interest of 40.2%. NGCP is the private concessionaire that operates the country’s electricity transmission network, with the remaining 40% owned by China’s State Grid Corporation.

The development comes more than a year and nine months after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. personally witnessed the signing of the agreement between MIC chief executive officer Rafael Consing Jr. and SGP chairman Henry Sy Jr. at Malacañang on January 27, 2025.

blocks.caption: DEAL? President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. with MIC president and CEO Rafael Consing Jr. (left) and SGP chairman Henry Sy Jr. (right). Photo from Philippine Communications Office.

blocks.text: Under the agreement, MIC was supposed to acquire a 20% stake in SGP through convertible preferred shares. This would entitle the sovereign wealth fund to two board seats each in SGP and NGCP, giving the government greater access to information and influence over the privately operated transmission grid.
Consing had initially expected the transaction documents to be signed within 90 days, with a possible 90-day extension.

The canceled transaction is separate from MIC’s existing investment in SGP. MIC had already invested P1.2 billion in the listed company’s shares through stock market purchases, generating P589.2 million in dividends and unrealized gains that year.
The reported collapse of the deal comes as Consing approaches the end of his three-year term in November. No successor has been formally named.

The sovereign wealth fund, whose creation was dogged by controversy over governance safeguards, has had a slow and shaky start. By the end of 2025, Maharlika had invested just P5.9 billion of the initial P75 billion contributed by two state-owned banks.

Investments picked up in 2026, bringing cumulative capital deployment to P24.7 billion as of June, or about a third of its initial funding. However, P15 billion of that amount came from a working capital facility extended to Petron Corporation, while MIC still held P53 billion in cash and cash equivalents. – Rappler.com

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No, Marcos can’t be arrested for P50-M bounty on Dela Rosa
articles.summary: An incumbent president enjoys immunity from suit while in office

blocks.text: Claim: The Filipino people can now arrest President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for fraud and bribery, specifically for pushing for Senator Bato dela Rosa’s arrest by putting a P50-million bounty on his head.
Why we fact-checked this: Makata Ng Bayan, a Facebook user with 1.1 million followers, posted a photo bearing the claim on October 26.

The photo contains text that reads: “Pwede ng arestuhin ng taong bayan si Marcos sa kasong fraud at bribery! Dahil sa panunuhol ng 50 milyon para gipitin si Bato gamit ang pera ng bayan without Philippine warrant.”
(The public can now arrest Marcos for fraud and bribery — specifically for the P50-million bribe used to corner Bato, using public funds without a Philippine warrant.)

The author of the post then wrote: “Pakikalat ng mensahe! Isa ka ba sa matapang na handang umaresto kay Marcos?” (Please spread the message! Are you one of the brave individuals prepared to arrest Marcos?)
Multiple users have already reposted or shared the photo. Commenters have mocked Marcos while taunting others to arrest him.
The post garnered 48,200 reactions, 8,400 comments, and 14,000 shares as of writing.

The facts: Marcos cannot be arrested or sued in any civil, criminal, or administrative case while he is president. There is also no warrant of arrest against him for alleged fraud and bribery mentioned in the claim.
An incumbent president enjoys immunity from suit. Although not explicitly mentioned in the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court recognizes an incumbent president’s immunity while serving in office.

This principle protects the president’s ability to carry out his or her responsibilities free from any distractions. Once his or her term ends, the former president may immediately be subject to any civil, criminal, or administrative complaints in relation to incidents before or during his or her presidency.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro also confirmed on October 27 that Marcos did not personally authorize the bounty. It was Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla who ordered it.
On October 23, the DILG and the Philippine National Police gave Dela Rosa a one-week deadline to surrender, then offered a P50-million reward for those who could help capture him.

In an interview with Radyo Pilipinas and as quoted in an Inquirer.NET story, Castro said, “It’s not like the President will specifically mention giving him a P50-million bounty. That won’t come from the President himself because this is a strategy, an operation by Secretary Jonvic Remulla and the PNP leadership.”
Warrant for Dela Rosa: There is a legitimate warrant out for Dela Rosa from the International Criminal Court (ICC) for crimes against humanity, alongside former president Rodrigo Duterte.

This international warrant is valid because it covers the period when the country was still a member of the ICC and when drug war killings were still happening. This is provided for in Article 127 of the Rome Statute, which says that a country’s withdrawal of membership does not affect cooperation with ongoing criminal proceedings that had already started before the withdrawal took effect. A member-country’s withdrawal takes effect a year after receipt by the UN Secretary-General of the notification.
On October 28, Dela Rosa’s camp asked the Supreme Court to reverse its earlier decision that denied their plea for a restraining order to prevent use of the arrest warrant against the senator.
Other fact checks: Rappler has already debunked multiple claims surrounding Dela Rosa’s arrest:

items: FACT CHECK: No basis for claim that Bato Dela Rosa is under Trump’s protection
FACT CHECK: Bato dela Rosa not removed from Senate
FACT CHECK: Bato dela Rosa not yet arrested; online posts misuse old video
FACT CHECK: Bato dela Rosa not at recent INC rallies; post uses January 2025 video
FACT CHECK: Post misuses news report to claim ICC arrest warrant vs Dela Rosa is fake

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Ombudsman suspends 2 QC brgy. execs over P22.28M unsettled disallowances, ghost projects
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has slapped a six-month preventive suspension against Quezon City Quirino 3B (Claro) Punong Barangay Ronald Tagle and Barangay Treasurer Richelle Ann Santillan over…

blocks.text: Published October 30, 2026 4:12pm

The Office of the Ombudsman has slapped a six-month preventive suspension against Quezon City Quirino 3B (Claro) Punong Barangay Ronald Tagle and Barangay Treasurer Richelle Ann Santillan over alleged unsettled audit disallowances and non-existent projects.

In a five-page order, the Ombudsman found that the evidence of guilt against the respondents was strong, citing Commission on Audit (COA) findings which showed non-submission of required supporting documents, as well as irregularities in the utilization, documentation, and processing of barangay funds, including non-submission of supporting documents for such fund utilization.
“Tagle, in conspiracy with Santillan, withdrew the savings of Barangay Quirino 3B (Claro) from 2018 to 2023 for non-existent or ghost projects,” the order read.
Specifically, the Ombudsman said that P1.4 million worth of procurement transactions in 2017 and 2018 were unsupported by complete documentation.
The Ombudsman also cited the following undocumented disbursements under the watch of the respondents:

items: P15.9 million in 2020
P23.9 million in 2021
P17.64 million in 2022 and
P17.88 million in 2023

blocks.text: Further the Ombudsman said that Tagle and Santillan authorized the release of P22.7 million of public funds without the required disbursement vouchers, resulting in COA's issuance of notices of disallowance.

“Respondents' administrative violation appears to be supported by evidence. The evidence on record shows that the guilt of respondents is strong, the charges against them involve Grave Misconduct, and Gross Neglect of Duty,” the Ombudsman said.
"The charges against them involved offenses that may warrant removal from service, and their continued stay in office could prejudice the administrative proceedings," the order added.
The complaint against the barangay officials was filed by the Office of the Ombudsman’s Field Investigation Office.

The anti-graft body tasked Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte to immediately implement the preventive suspension and inform the Office of the Ombudsman of the action taken within three days of receipt of the order.

Sought for comment, Tagle and Santillan told GMA News Online via phone call that they are continuously addressing the COA findings and have filed a motion for reconsideration before the Ombudsman on October 30. —AOL, GMA News
